title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) to measure whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating under shared_initial_candidate semantics. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents using a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. We describe the preregistered design and execution, interpret the artifact‑grounded degenerate null result, identify concrete contributors to the ceiling effect, and provide artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that avoid this degeneracy.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configuration sequences and maintenance workflows. For operational adoption, it is critical to show that model outputs will not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied in production. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that safety depends heavily on surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than on the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures combining generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited.

Research question. Under shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one sampled candidate reused by both arms), does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals compared with observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a deterministic NetOps validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents under shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an interpretation of the ceiling effect grounded in archived artifacts; and (5) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs to produce nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research spans intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, RCA, and agentic automation proposals [1]–[4]. Surveys document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[3]. Work on LLM‑assisted DevOps and program repair demonstrates that downstream deterministic checks plus repair loops can improve safety or repairability in those domains under specific datasets and validators; representative verified examples include an LLM‑based DevOps copilot evaluation and autonomous program‑repair work that report improvements conditional on validator/test harness coverage [5],[6].

Methodological gaps motivating our design. First, pipeline comparisons that allow different first‑pass model draws per arm confound validator effects with model sampling variance. Second, many existing benchmarks emphasize QA/relevance or log/RCA metrics but lack tightly coupled intent→config items evaluated under deterministic validators with paired protocols that preserve initial candidate sampling. Our shared_initial_candidate experiment isolates validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates and therefore directly addresses the first gap while highlighting how generation semantics shape inference.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. The study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and froze the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline); generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate; model/adaptor = gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; gate policy and repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents); and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). The preregistration and configuration files are archived in the execution manifest.

Generation semantics clarification. The executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded arms per paired intent. Consequently, the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on that identical first‑pass candidate and does not measure effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or model sampling variance.

Models, adapter, validator, and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini" and provider="openai_responses"). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks (sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency). The recorded model configuration includes max_output_tokens=2000, maximum_attempts_per_call=1, reasoning_effort="minimal", and temperature=null. Explicitly: temperature=null was used in the recorded model configuration; null/unset temperature is not evidence of deterministic sampling (it does not imply temperature=0), and the adapter does not guarantee deterministic model sampling. The shared_initial_candidate semantics were implemented by requesting one model generation per pair and reusing that single sampled output for both arms.

Task bank and deterministic sampling. The deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced intents with embedded constraints (allowed_fields, allowed_touched_fields, preserve_unspecified_state, workflow_policies) and explicit required_sequence lists. The preregistered sampler selected 200 paired intents using the adapter's deterministic index rule; selection is fixed prior to model calls and outcome‑independent. Per‑task difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard", "extreme") and full task payloads are archived in the task manifest.

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: inspect the shared initial candidate (no gating). Guarded: submit the identical shared candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the deterministic gate followed a preregistered accept/reject rule and allowed up to one automated repair attempt when violations were detected. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization; scoring used rule full_intent_constraint_validation and yielded codes such as VALID_CONFIGURATION. Per‑episode validator traces (validation_before/validation_after), repair flags, and scoring outputs were archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed as preregistered (execution manifest): start 2026‑08‑31T13:49:34 UTC; end 2026‑08‑31T14:14:32 UTC. Planned_episode_count = 400; completed_episode_count = 400; failed_episode_count = 0. Model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair); hosted_model_call_event_count = 200; cache_hit_count = 0; cache_miss_count = 200. Deterministic reconciliation asserts episode_accounting_consistent = true.

Primary confirmatory outcome (artifact‑grounded). The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) is n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Thus every shared initial candidate was scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms. The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0. Exact two‑sided test: p = 1.0. Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0,0.0] using bootstrap_seed=1729 and 10,000 resamples. The zero‑width CI and p=1.0 follow directly from perfect concordance (no discordant pairs).

Repair activity and diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in the scoring artifacts. Representative episodes (task‑000004–task‑000008) show parsed_command_count == required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count consistent with task payloads, and validation_after.valid = true. Validator traces record final_state snapshots, parsed commands, and violation_count = 0 for all episodes.

Missingness and contamination. Missingness_summary: complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes. Contamination_summary is empty (no flagged contamination). Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 200 and all deterministic consistency checks passed.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation of the degenerate null. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 indicates that, for the chosen LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic task bank, the prompt/templates used, and the validator ruleset, the sampled initial candidates already satisfied the validator constraints; therefore the guarded machinery applied no repairs and altered no acceptance decisions. The archived artifacts (paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/scoring/*.json) directly support this interpretation.

Why the paired bootstrap CI is zero‑width. With no discordant pairs every bootstrap resample yields the same paired difference (0.0), producing zero empirical variance and thus CI = [0.0,0.0]. This is an inferentially legitimate outcome recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000).

Ceiling‑effect contributors (artifact‑traceable). The artifacts point to three contributors: (1) task‑bank alignment—the deterministic task generator synthesized intents with required_sequences closely matching the expected prompt schema, increasing the probability of syntactically correct outputs (task manifest entries include required_sequence lists and workflow_policies); (2) validator tightness—the validator's rules encoded sequencing and precondition checks matching the task generator's constraints so correct syntactic mappings passed validation readily (validator traces show parsed_command_count == required_command_count in representative episodes); and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that might have produced repairs or discordant outcomes. Each contributor is traceable in archived artifacts.

Design recommendations grounded in execution artifacts. To obtain nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value we recommend preregistered changes that are immediately actionable from the archived bundle: (a) increase baseline unsafe rates by augmenting the task bank with out‑of‑distribution or adversarial seeds (the manifest encodes generation_seed and difficulty labels that can be modified to inject adversarial seeds); (b) switch to independent per‑condition generation (two independent model calls per pair) or multiple samples per condition to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model variance—this increases model_call accounting (e.g., up to 400 calls for a two‑call regime with 200 pairs); (c) test multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to expose sampling variance (execution/model_configuration.json records requested_model and temperature fields and can be adapted); (d) increase the automated repair budget or enable iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness once initial violations are nontrivial; and (e) add human‑in‑the‑loop arms to measure operator responses to validator flags. These options are executable without inventing new verifier code and are directly supported by the archived manifests.

Operational caveats. The null result does not imply deterministic validators lack value in more adversarial or production regimes; it demonstrates that experimental design choices (task bank, generation semantics, validator rules) determine whether a shared‑candidate paired contrast can detect verifier value. Field deployments require adversarial testing, independent generation regimes, multi‑model comparisons, and HITL evaluations to quantify operational benefits.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result is specific to the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the synthetic deterministically selected task bank, the validator ruleset, and the shared_initial_candidate semantics; it does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different experimental regimes (e.g., independent per‑condition generation, adversarial inputs, multiple model samples) [1]–[6]. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions. All core artifacts and analysis outputs supporting these conclusions are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle.

disclosure_statement: This study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and executed autonomously after the autonomy lock. Model and tools: single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration/adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Human role and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topical family and constrained the initial prompt pre‑lock; all literature review, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review emulation, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the lock. Generation semantics: the executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. A full execution and analysis artifact bundle is archived with the preregistration; the bundle contains the raw model responses, per‑episode validator traces, task manifest, model configuration, and analysis outputs.
limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions or vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
